unit.title: Trail basics
unit.summary: What a hike is, how routes are shaped, how trails are marked, and how to share them.

lessons.title: What counts as a hike
lessons.objective: You can tell a day hike from a walk in the park and know why the trailhead matters.

payload.prompt: What makes a trailhead different from a parking lot at a park?

options.text: Trailheads always have a fee
A trailhead marks the official start of a marked trail with parking and usually a sign
Trailheads are only in national parks
A trailhead is just a random place you park

explanation.correct: A trailhead is the marked start point with parking, a sign, and often a register or trail map. It tells hikers where the route actually begins.
explanation.incorrect: Some trailheads have fees and some don't. They exist on all kinds of land, not just parks. The key is the sign and the organized parking area.
explanation.sayThisLine: Meet me at the trailhead by 6:30. The lot fills up by eight.

payload.prompt: What does a trailhead give you?

pairs.definition: Where the marked trail begins
A place to leave your car so it's not miles away when you return
A sign or map showing the trail name, distance and sometimes rules
A log where hikers sign in so rangers know who was there

distractorDefinitions: A place to buy snacks and water

explanation.summary: A trailhead is the organized entry point: parking, a sign, and sometimes a register book. It's how you know you're in the right place.
explanation.sayThisLine: The trailhead has a register. Sign it so rangers know the trail is being used.

payload.prompt: You see a parking lot with a single sign that says 'Trail Closed.' Should you start hiking?

scene.alt: A parking lot with a wooden sign reading 'Trail Closed' at the trailhead.

explanation.correct: A trailhead sign that says closed means it's closed. Respect the sign: the trail may be unsafe, under repair, or closed for wildlife protection.
explanation.incorrect: Trailhead signs convey official information. Closed means closed. Always respect trail markers and signs.
explanation.sayThisLine: The sign says closed, so we do not hike it. Maybe next month.

payload.prompt: Complete the sentences.
payload.template: A trailhead is more organized than a {{random}} parking lot because it has a {{info}} and {{space}}.

explanation.correct: A trailhead has a sign that tells you trail info and parking reserved for hikers. It marks the official start clearly.
explanation.incorrect: Trailheads stand out because they are organized with a sign, parking and often a register. Random parking lacks these markers.

lessons.title: Shapes of a route
lessons.objective: You can name out-and-back, loop, lollipop and point-to-point and say what each demands.

payload.prompt: Match each route shape to its description.

pairs.definition: Go to a point, return the same way
Returns to the start without retracing
Stem in, loop at the far end, stem back out
Ends somewhere else; needs a shuttle or two cars

distractorDefinitions: A trail with no defined route

explanation.summary: Each shape has different logistics. An out-and-back means you know the way back. A loop avoids retracing. A lollipop adds a loop at the top. Point-to-point needs a getaway.
explanation.sayThisLine: Is it a loop or an out-and-back? That changes the whole plan.

payload.prompt: Tap the lollipop route shape.

diagram.alt: Four trail route shapes shown: an out-and-back going up and down, a loop circle, a lollipop with a straight stem and loop at top, and a point-to-point diagonal line

explanation.correct: A lollipop is a stem going in and a loop at the far end before coming back out the same stem.
explanation.incorrect: A loop circles back to the start. A lollipop has a straight stem and then a loop at the end, like the candy.
explanation.sayThisLine: It's a lollipop: two miles up the stem, then the loop around the lake.

payload.prompt: You plan an out-and-back hike but see an alternative point-to-point route. What do you need to do differently?

options.text: Arrange a shuttle or two cars so you end up somewhere different
Plan to reverse the route and hike the same way back
Connect it to a loop to get back to the start
Overnight camp at the endpoint

explanation.correct: A point-to-point route ends somewhere else, so you need logistics: a shuttle service, a second car, or someone to pick you up.
explanation.incorrect: That is what makes point-to-point different from out-and-back. You need a way to get home from the endpoint.
explanation.sayThisLine: A point-to-point means a shuttle or two cars, otherwise we just hike to the car we left.

payload.prompt: You are halfway through a loop hike and realize you do not like this trail. Can you skip the second half and hike back to the car a different way?

scene.alt: A loop trail with your location marked at the top, showing the path you came from and the remaining loop ahead.

choices.label: No, complete the loop or backtrack

explanation.correct: Stay on marked trails. Either finish the loop or backtrack the way you came. Shortcuts create erosion and social trails.
explanation.incorrect: Leaving a loop halfway risks getting lost and creates erosion problems. Finish the loop or backtrack to the car.
explanation.sayThisLine: We finished the loop even though we were tired. Better to stay on the trail than cut across.

lessons.title: Trail furniture
lessons.objective: You can recognize a junction, a spur and a switchback and explain why each exists.

payload.prompt: What is this trail feature?

image.alt: Aerial view of a trail zigzagging up a steep slope with many hairpin turns.

options.text: Switchbacks, hairpin turns to climb steep ground
A spur trail to a viewpoint
A loop where trails cross
The most direct line to the top

explanation.correct: These zigzags are switchbacks. They trade distance for a gentler grade, sparing your legs and the hillside from direct erosion.
explanation.incorrect: A switchback is a hairpin turn that lets steep slopes be hiked at a gentler grade. That back-and-forth pattern is the whole point.
explanation.sayThisLine: Forty switchbacks. I counted. Twice.
cues: Goes up a steep slope in zigzags

payload.prompt: Fill in the blanks.
payload.template: A {{place}} is where trails meet and an easy place to go wrong. A {{short}} is a quick detour to a lake or viewpoint.

explanation.correct: A junction is a trail intersection where the right choice matters. A spur is a marked branch off the main trail, often worth a quick visit.
explanation.incorrect: Junctions are where you can take a wrong turn. Spurs are official side trails, not social trails (which are eroded shortcuts).

payload.prompt: At a junction you see a sign: 'Waterfall Spur, 0.5 miles.' What does this tell you?

options.text: It is an official side trail you can take and return on
It is a shortcut that skips part of the main trail
It is closed to the public
It is dangerous and only for experts

explanation.correct: A spur is an official branch with a sign and distance. You can take it as a detour and return to the main trail the same way. It adds miles to your day.
explanation.incorrect: A spur is marked and maintained, not a shortcut. It is a side trip to a feature like a waterfall or viewpoint that the trail crew wants you to see.

payload.prompt: Match each trail feature to its purpose.

pairs.definition: Where two or more trails meet and you must choose a direction
An official side route to a waterfall, viewpoint or camp with its own sign
A hairpin turn that climbs steep ground at a gentler angle

explanation.summary: A junction is a choice point, a spur is a marked detour and a switchback is a gentle climb on steep ground. Each serves a different purpose on the trail.
explanation.sayThisLine: We took the spur left to the outlook, came back and finished the main trail with its switchbacks.

payload.prompt: At a junction you spot what looks like an unmarked shortcut down the slope. Should you take it?
payload.context: You are tired, the junction is busy with other hikers, and the shortcut would save 20 minutes.

options.text: Take the shortcut to save time
Stay on the marked trail even though it is longer
Ask other hikers if they know the shortcut
Send one person to scout it quickly

explanation.correct: Stay on marked trails. Unmarked shortcuts cause erosion and can get you lost or injured. The extra 20 minutes is worth staying safe.
explanation.incorrect: Shortcuts create social trails that erode slopes and confuse other hikers. Even if others have used it, it is still off-trail.
explanation.sayThisLine: We were tired but we stayed on the marked trail. Social trails hurt the mountain.
explanation.safetyNote: Hiking off-trail risks getting lost, damaging the environment, and potentially falling on unstable ground. Stay on marked trails even if longer.

lessons.title: Following the marks
lessons.objective: You can read blazes and cairns and spot a social trail.

payload.prompt: What does this double blaze mean?

image.alt: Two stacked white paint blazes on a tree, the top one shifted to the right of the lower one.

options.text: Continue straight
A turn is coming, the top blaze points the way
You are at the summit
The trail is closed

explanation.correct: Two blazes stacked with the upper one offset signal a change of direction in many systems, including the Appalachian Trail. Stay alert.
explanation.incorrect: A single blaze means continue. Two stacked with an offset warns of a turn, in the direction the upper blaze is shifted.
explanation.sayThisLine: Double blaze, so the trail turns here.
cues: Top blaze offset to one side
Offset points the direction of the turn

payload.prompt: You see a barely visible path and a stack of stones nearby. What should you follow?

options.text: The stone stack (cairn)
The worn path (probably a social trail)
Stop and check your map
Follow both at the same time

explanation.correct: Cairns mark the official route on bare rock or above treeline. Social trails are shortcuts that hikers have worn into the ground but are not maintained and cause erosion.
explanation.incorrect: A stack of stones is a trail marker placed deliberately. A worn path might look like a trail but could be an eroded social trail. Cairns are the official route.
explanation.sayThisLine: Follow the cairns across the slab, and please don't build new ones.

payload.prompt: Match each marker or trail type to its meaning.

pairs.definition: A paint mark on a tree or rock showing the official trail direction
A stack of stones used to mark the trail on bare rock or above treeline
An eroded shortcut created by hikers but not maintained or marked officially

distractorDefinitions: A warning sign posted by rangers

explanation.summary: Blazes and cairns are official markers that guide you on the right path. Social trails are unofficial shortcuts that damage the land.
explanation.sayThisLine: I followed the blazes and then the cairns once we got above the trees.

payload.prompt: Complete the sentence.
payload.template: A single {{mark}} means keep going straight, but a {{double}} warns that the trail is about to {{turn}}.

explanation.correct: A single blaze tells you the trail continues straight. Two stacked blazes, especially if offset, signal a sharp turn coming.
explanation.incorrect: Blaze systems vary, but a double blaze almost always means stay alert for a direction change. Look carefully at the offset to find the turn.

payload.prompt: Tap the cairn that marks the official trail on this boulder field.

diagram.alt: A boulder field with three stacked stone piles. One is an official cairn with distinct layering, one is a natural pile of loose stones, and one is partially collapsed.

explanation.correct: An official cairn is carefully stacked with distinct layers and placed at trail junctions to mark the route. It stands out from random stone piles.
explanation.incorrect: Official cairns are built deliberately and stand apart. Natural piles are random; collapsed ones may have been cairns but are no longer reliable.
explanation.sayThisLine: Follow that cairn. Someone built it to mark the trail through these rocks.

lessons.title: Who yields to whom
lessons.objective: You can call right of way correctly on a narrow trail.

payload.prompt: You are heading downhill. A hiker climbs toward you.

scene.alt: Narrow trail on a slope. You stand upslope and another hiker climbs toward you.

explanation.correct: Customarily the uphill hiker has the right of way: they are working harder and it is harder to restart momentum.
explanation.incorrect: The common courtesy is that the descending hiker yields. If the trail is wide or they wave you through, thank them and pass.
explanation.sayThisLine: Go ahead, you've got the hill.

payload.prompt: A mountain biker approaches you uphill. Who should step aside?

options.text: You (the hiker) should step aside
The biker should step aside
The trail is wide enough for both
It depends if there are horses

explanation.correct: Bikes yield to hikers, and hikers yield to horses. It's about who is working hardest and who needs the most help staying on the trail.
explanation.incorrect: The hierarchy is: bikes yield to hikers, hikers yield to horses. Horses always have the right of way.
explanation.sayThisLine: I stepped off for the bike. The hierarchy is clear: bikes give way to us, we give way to horses.

payload.prompt: Match each group to their right of way on a narrow trail.

pairs.definition: Always have the right of way; most easily spooked
Yield to horses, have right of way over bikes
Yield to both hikers and horses

explanation.summary: The hierarchy is: horses first, then hikers, then bikes. It is based on who is hardest to control and who needs the most space.
explanation.sayThisLine: I stepped to the side: the hierarchy is horses, hikers, bikes. No debate.

payload.prompt: Two hikers with a loaded pack mule approach you going downhill on a narrow trail. What do you do?
payload.context: The trail has a steep drop. There is a small pull-out 20 feet behind you but none ahead of them.

options.text: Move back to the pull-out and let them pass
Stay put and let them figure it out
Wave them back up the trail
Walk faster down to clear the trail

explanation.correct: A pack animal has the highest right of way. Move back to the pull-out if you are downhill. Give them the easy path even if you have to back up.
explanation.incorrect: Pack animals are less predictable than hikers and harder to control. Respect the hierarchy: move out of their way, especially on narrow terrain.
explanation.sayThisLine: A mule has the right of way. We walked back to the wider spot and let them through.
explanation.safetyNote: Pack animals can spook easily on narrow trails. Always move to give them the safest, widest path possible.

statement.speaker: Alex
statement.text: I always step aside for anyone coming uphill. It just makes sense.

options.text: The uphill hiker is working harder and has less momentum to restart
It is just basic trail courtesy
Downhill hikers get tired more easily
Downhill hikers are faster

payload.translation: He gives way to uphill hikers because they are working harder against gravity and need their momentum.

followUps.line: Do you hike with people who forget the rule?
Have you ever had someone refuse to step aside?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: It is fine to ask or offer to move. Trail right of way is about safety and kindness, not knowing every rule perfectly.

lessons.title: Leave No Trace, plainly
lessons.objective: You can explain the seven principles and give one everyday example each.

payload.prompt: You are tired and want to rest. Where should you sit?

options.text: On bare rock or gravel (a durable surface)
On moss or alpine plants
On green grass or wildflowers
On a tree stump or fallen log

explanation.correct: Durable surfaces are rock, gravel, maintained trail and hard-packed ground. They can handle human use without damage.
explanation.incorrect: Moss, plants and soft ground get trampled and take decades to recover. Rock and gravel are designed to be walked on.
explanation.sayThisLine: We rested on the slickrock, it's a durable surface, not the moss.

payload.prompt: You finish an apple at the top and see the core. Do you?
payload.context: It is biodegradable. The peak is a popular site. You are two hours from the trailhead.

options.text: Leave it, it will break down in a few months
Pack it out in your trash bag
Throw it down the slope where no one will see it
Dig a small hole and bury it

explanation.correct: Pack it out. Cores last months to years and other hikers don't want to see or smell it. Fruit peels are trash that must be carried out.
explanation.incorrect: Even biodegradable items need to be packed out to keep the peak clean, preserve the soil and avoid attracting animals.
explanation.sayThisLine: Orange peels are trash too. Pack it out.
explanation.safetyNote: Leave No Trace is not just about looks—it is about protecting the wilderness for others and for wildlife.

payload.prompt: Match each example to the Leave No Trace principle it follows.

pairs.definition: Stay on rock, gravel or hardpan, not on living plants or soft soil

pairs.term: Pack it out, all of it
pairs.definition: Carry every wrapper, core, and piece of trash home
Use established fire rings or cook on stoves instead of making new fires

distractorDefinitions: Hike at night to see fewer people
Tell everyone about the best spots

explanation.summary: Leave No Trace means respecting the land by using durable surfaces, packing out everything and minimizing your footprint.
explanation.sayThisLine: We camped on the rock shelf, packed every scrap and used our stove so no fires needed.

payload.prompt: Finish these statements.
payload.template: On a {{high}} mountain, a {{durable}} surface is better to camp on than {{soft}}. You should {{pack}} all trash including {{items}}.

explanation.correct: Durable surfaces like rock and hardpan can handle use. Soft soil and plants take decades to recover. Pack out all trash, even fruit.
explanation.incorrect: Every scrap you leave behind affects the trail and the animals. Rock and gravel are durable. Soil and plants are fragile.

payload.prompt: You see a beautiful alpine meadow with wildflowers. Can you walk through it to get a better photo?

scene.alt: An alpine meadow with blooming wildflowers and a trail cutting through it.

choices.label: Yes, stay just off the trail
No, take photos from the trail

explanation.correct: Stay on the trail even in beautiful meadows. One person walking off-trail crushes plants. Many people destroy the meadow. Photos from the trail are enough.
explanation.incorrect: Alpine plants take decades to grow and are fragile. Stepping on them once damages them. Respect the meadow by staying on the trail.
explanation.sayThisLine: It looks great from the trail. Stepping off kills the flowers we want others to enjoy too.

statement.speaker: Jordan
statement.text: I always pack out my trash, even the biodegradable stuff.

options.text: It attracts animals and changes their natural diet
Others don't want to see it on the trail
Biodegradable items break down very slowly at altitude
It is easier to throw away at home

payload.translation: He packs out everything because even natural items attract animals, take years to break down at altitude and make the trail less appealing.

followUps.line: What was the hardest thing you have packed out?
followUps.why: Curious about real-world Leave No Trace practice.

followUps.line: Have you seen trash that bothered you on a trail?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Packing out trash is simple. You do not need to be an expert to respect the wilderness.

lessons.title: A hike day, start to finish
lessons.objective: You can order a hike day from planning to the trail register and home.

payload.prompt: Order a well-run hike day.

items.why: Decide go or no-go before leaving.

items.text: Share your trip plan with someone

items.why: Pack for the worst plausible day.

items.text: Sign the trail register and start
items.why: A record of your route and time.

items.text: Turn back at your turnaround time
Tell your contact you are back
items.why: Closes the loop so nobody searches.

explanation.correct: A good day starts before the trailhead and ends with a check-in.
explanation.incorrect: The order matters: forecast and plan come before the walk, and check-in closes the loop so nobody starts a search.
explanation.sayThisLine: I text my sister my plan before I leave and when I'm back.

statement.speaker: A hiker
statement.text: I always sign the register when I get to the trailhead.

options.text: Rangers use it to know the trail is being used
It helps rescuers find you if you go missing
It helps count hikers visiting the area
It's just a fun memento book

payload.translation: She signs the register to leave a record so land managers know the trail is used and rescue can find her if something goes wrong.

followUps.line: Do you write notes in the register or just sign your name?
Have you ever found funny entries?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Signing in is a simple safety practice. You can ask what the register is for if you have not seen one.

payload.prompt: You arrive at the trailhead and the register is full. What should you do?

options.text: Skip signing since there is no room
Write your name on the back or ask if there is a new book
Take a photo to prove you were there
Text the ranger your plan instead

explanation.correct: Full registers mean many hikers. Look for a back page or a new book inside the box. A ranger should replace a full register regularly.
explanation.incorrect: A complete register shows the trail is popular. Keep looking for a place to sign or ask at the ranger station before leaving.

payload.prompt: Match each part of a well-run hike day to its purpose.

pairs.definition: Tell someone where you are going and when you expect to return
Leave a record at the trailhead with your name and the time you started
Text or call your contact when you return so no one starts a search

distractorDefinitions: Tell everyone about your route online

explanation.summary: A safe hike day starts with a plan, includes a register signature and ends with a check-in. Three steps, three circles of safety.
explanation.sayThisLine: I told my sister where I was going, signed the register and texted her when I was back.

payload.prompt: You reach the trailhead but realize you forgot to tell anyone where you are going. Do you?
payload.context: You are already there, the weather is perfect, and you only planned a short 3-hour hike.

options.text: Hike anyway, it is short
Call or text someone your plan before starting
Just sign the register, that is enough
Leave your plan on the dashboard of your car

explanation.correct: Stop and contact someone. The register is helpful but not enough. A personal contact knows you specifically and can alert rescuers if needed.
explanation.incorrect: Short hikes are where accidents happen just as much as long ones. Always tell someone your plan before you start, no matter the distance.
explanation.sayThisLine: I made the call before I left the parking lot. Five minutes to tell my brother my plan.
explanation.safetyNote: A trail register and a personal contact serve different purposes. You need both: the register for land managers and your contact for rescue.

lessons.title: First trail small talk
lessons.objective: You can respond to a hiker's trip recap with a curious, honest follow-up.

statement.speaker: Maya
statement.text: Fifteen switchbacks, then the ridge. My quads are still mad.

options.text: A steep climb with many hairpin turns
A long flat crest to walk
A weather problem
A gear complaint

payload.translation: She climbed a steep slope via zigzags, reached a ridge and is tired but happy.

followUps.line: How was the ridge, worth it?
followUps.why: Shows you heard the payoff, not just the pain.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Ask what a switchback is if you are unsure. Curiosity beats bluffing.

payload.title: Got turned around
payload.setting: She made a mistake and found the trail again

exchanges.theirMessage: I went left at a junction instead of right. Lost the trail for five minutes till I saw a blaze.

replies.text: At least you spotted a blaze and knew you could backtrack.
replies.theirResponse: Right, and I was paying attention. Turned right back.
replies.coachNote: You acknowledged she handled it well.

replies.theirResponse: Yeah, but it was weird to lose it so fast.
replies.coachNote: True, but ask what helped her get back.

replies.text: You should have looked at your map.
replies.theirResponse: I did, that's how I got back on.
replies.coachNote: She already handled it well. Ask how she fixed it.

exchanges.theirMessage: Junctions will get you every time.

replies.text: They are tricky because you have to choose. Do you mark them on your map?
I never get lost. I am good with maps.
replies.coachNote: Do not brag about your own skills during her story.

payload.closingNote: Listening means asking what she learned and what helped.

payload.prompt: Someone says 'We followed the blazes the whole way.' What does that tell you?

options.text: They stayed on the marked trail the whole time
They hiked quickly
They got turned around and had to backtrack
They found a shortcut

explanation.correct: Following the blazes means they stuck to the official marked trail. It is a sign of a well-navigated hike.
explanation.incorrect: Blazes are paint marks that show the official route. If someone followed them, they did not get lost.

payload.prompt: Match each term to what a hiker might say about it.

pairs.definition: A paint mark on a tree that shows you are on the right trail
A place where two trails meet and you have to choose
A zigzag path that climbs steep ground gently

explanation.summary: A hiker uses blazes to stay on track, navigates junctions with care and counts switchbacks when climbing steep slopes.
explanation.sayThisLine: The blazes led us right. At the junction we went left, then up through the switchbacks.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: The double blaze threw me off. I was looking for a single one.

options.text: A double blaze means a sharp turn is coming up
It is a warning to slow down or be careful
It means you are at the end of the trail
It means the trail is dangerous

payload.translation: He missed the warning because a double blaze signals a direction change, often sharp, that hikers need to anticipate.

followUps.line: Have you missed a turn despite the blazes?
Do you look ahead for blazes or just follow?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Missing blazes happens to everyone. The trick is to scan ahead for the next one after each turn.
